notes.title: The look — the draft's own words
notes.content:
>THE LOOK<

Tokyo as a memory that is still happening.

The city in this film belongs to no single year. Pay phones beside smartphones. Boxy CRT televisions glowing in shop windows. Showa-era vending machines humming on empty corners beneath new glass towers. None of it is ever commented on. It is simply how the world is.

LIGHT. The city lights the characters, not the sky: vending machines, shop signs, train windows, fluorescent tubes. Sodium orange against a sick fluorescent green. Soft halation around every light, blacks slightly crushed. It should look like film, and feel like something remembered.

RAIN. Never glamorous. No lightning, no storms. Cold, steady, patient rain that turns the streets black and reflective.

CAMERA. Wide and patient. Close-ups are rare, so they count. We watch people inside the city, not apart from it.

SOUND. Real Tokyo sounds, placed slightly wrong: a crossing melody for an empty street, a television laughing in an empty room. Music arrives late, and sparingly.

OTHER LIVES. There is always a sign of other people -- a lit window, a radio through a wall, laundry overhead. Every private moment happens among thousands of others.

!NOTHING IS EXPLAINED.

LANGUAGE. The Voss sisters speak English to each other. Dialogue marked (in Japanese) is spoken in Japanese and subtitled in English.

REFERENCE POINTS. Ozu's TOKYO STORY for restraint. KOWLOON GENERIC ROMANCE and the 1997 illustrated Kowloon Walled City panoramas for density, texture and memory.

notes.title: The style block — what every frame is generated with
notes.content:
Every keyframe in this workspace is generated with the same style block, attached cast sheets where the sisters appear, and the same negative prompt. The block is also the **Neo-Noir Tokyo** entry in the app's visual-style library, so the prompt studio writes it into any batch you generate from this project.

**Style block**
cinematic film still, 16:9 full-bleed widescreen (1920×1080), shot on 35mm Kodak Vision3 500T, visible fine grain, soft halation around every light source, slightly crushed blacks, muted desaturated palette, romantic melancholy in a Tokyo that feels remembered rather than documented, a dark dangerous place made warm by human tenderness, longing, regret, and the ache of something beautiful already slipping into the past. The city belongs to no single year: Showa-era vending machines, hand-painted shop signs, tangled overhead power lines, payphones and older televisions beside smartphones, never explained, never a period piece, never sci-fi. Cold steady rain, wet black asphalt with long mirror reflections, practical light only — cold vending-machine white, sodium orange, sick fluorescent green, one warm window, a distant train full of strangers. Wide, patient, observational compositions with figures small and separated by the city, quiet as the default; sudden flat unglamorous violence is rare and punctures the stillness rather than becoming action spectacle. Crowded streets and rooms full of lives the characters cannot quite reach, foreigners half-belonging, romance and missed chances carried by ordinary objects, no moonlight, no theatrical emotion, no explanatory imagery, a world that exists only in memory.

**Negative prompt**
lightning, dramatic storm, glossy cyberpunk, holograms, flying cars, heavy neon overload, oversaturated colors, clean digital look, HDR, sharp CGI, bokeh overload, close-up portrait, fashion pose, smiling, anime style

**If a frame comes out too cyberpunk:** drop "neon" from the prompt and add *1990s*, *ordinary*, *worn*, *documentary realism*.

The nine keys generated from the brief are on the mood board *The style block — nine keys*, and the prompts themselves are recorded in `src/lib/styles.ts`.

notes.title: Continuity — the Voss family, and everyone else
notes.content:
**Mara Voss (24)** and **Vera Voss (29)** are American sisters: ash-blonde hair, pale blue eyes, distinct faces locked to sheets/mara.jpg and sheets/vera.jpg and their face crops. Mara's longer wavy hair is soaked flat in the opening; her cheap red-bird clip slides loose between the crates in scene 2 and is gone from that beat on. The final scene gives the clip to Vera.

Vera's opening wardrobe is charcoal wool coat, cream knit, navy trousers and brown boots. In scenes 72–75 she wears her mother's wine-red silk dress, broad straps, modest cowl neckline and calf-length bias-cut skirt. Her makeup is pretty, carefully applied and INTACT in the hotel, with dry groomed hair. Only rain in scene 73 washes it into thin mascara trails and plasters her fringe. Both red court shoes remain until the skid: thereafter RIGHT foot bare, LEFT shoe on. No coat or umbrella on the street; the folded pale-blue umbrella stays by the hotel stool.

**Jack (48)** is the private investigator and former police detective, not her father and never Jack Voss. The screenplay supplies no surname. Recast on 25 September 2026 as a white American, following the regenerated sheets/jack.jpg and jack-face.jpg: lean, long angular face, deep-set grey-green eyes, dark brown hair greying at the temples, salt-and-pepper stubble, a good badly kept charcoal overcoat over an off-white open-collar shirt. In the confrontation he is soaked, hands dark, no tie or weapon; he takes the blows and kneels apart after she pushes him away. Scene 74's three Jack frames have been regenerated with the recast (JACK RECAST APPLIED); every Jack frame now matches the new sheet. In scene 77 he is still in the wet coat, hands unwashed.

In scenes 78–79 Vera is barefoot, still in the creased red dress, hair dried, mascara dried; the umbrella stand is empty and both cups are empty. Daniel's notebook: small, worn dark-green cloth cover, DANIEL VOSS inside the cover.

**Daniel Voss (41, twenty years ago)** is the American father in the family photograph, identified by the scene 11 clipping. Daniel, not Jack, holds nine-year-old Vera's and four-year-old Mara's hands outside the noodle shop. The photograph asset itself is unchanged; the incorrect cast label and parent links are corrected.

The masked men never receive faces. The old man and journalist remain unnamed. Ishida and the young officer keep their existing sheets. Scene 75 has no people anywhere, including reflections.

notes.title: Language — English, Japanese, and the subtitles
notes.content:
The Voss sisters speak **English** to each other — including on the phone, including the answerphone message Vera cannot bring herself to answer.

Dialogue marked *(in Japanese)* is spoken in Japanese and subtitled in English, and it is never used for local colour: Mara's Japanese is halting and she is understood just barely; Vera's is fluent, careful and slightly formal, learned as a child and relearned as an adult; Ishida's English is excellent and she refuses it anyway, which is the only line either of them draws in the interview room. The old man's "twenty years" and "don't let them have it" are Japanese, and the masked man's two position reports are Japanese into a radio.

The audience is never told what the key opens, what the position reports are counting towards, or why the journalist had a notebook. Nothing is explained — that is the film's rule, and it is also the workspace's.

notes.title: What the keyframes are, and what they are not
notes.content:
**Format: every image is 16:9 full-bleed, 1920×1080 JPEG, no letterbox** — the final screenplay's rule for this film. Frames already on disk that were made at 2.39:1 (the older style keys only, which stay 2.39:1 references by design) are legacy studies awaiting that revision, not a licence to crop; regenerate, never reframe by cropping. Every frame in this storyboard is a **draft AI study** standing in for a shot that has not been photographed. They are generated in passes of ten, in screenplay order, from the boards in `docs/neonoire/scenes/` with the cast sheets attached as references.

They are useful for: framing, lens, blocking, light direction, wardrobe continuity, and seeing whether the scene plays in order in the animatic.

They are not: approved coverage, a lighting plan, a cast approval, or a licence to stop checking. Faces drift between passes more than anything else — if a study of Mara or Vera does not match her sheet, mark the frame **Needs review** and regenerate it. Each frame's notes carry the pass it came from.

notes.title: Frame format — images are 16:9

From the final screenplay (`Neonoire (3).fountain`) onward, **every image in this film is 16:9 full-bleed, 1920×1080 JPEG, no letterbox** — including every keyframe generated for scenes 8–100 as the board reaches them.

The studio look keeps its film character at the new shape: 35mm Kodak Vision3 500T grain, halation, crushed blacks, practical light — the Neo-Noir Tokyo style block in the app's library now opens with "16:9 full-bleed widescreen" instead of scope.

**Legacy exceptions: none remain in the numbered board.** As of 26 September 2026 every frame of every boarded scene — cold open, feature, scene 3 — is 16:9 full-bleed 1920×1080; only the older style keys 1–3 and 6–9 stay 2.39:1 references by design. Regenerate those in 16:9; never crop a revised frame back to scope, and never letterbox 16:9 content to fake it.

Normalise a fresh 16:9 frame with:

`convert FILE.jpg -resize "1920x1080^" -gravity center -extent 1920x1080 -quality 92 -strip FILE.jpg`

notes.title: Scenes 72–75 — Tokyo Story in colour
notes.content:
25 September 2026. Ten image-generation calls: Jack's new identity sheet plus nine shot replacements/new studies. Completed board shots: 69, 70, 72, 74, 75, 76, 77, 79, 80. Six placeholders await replacement: 71 (hotel exit), 73 (machine pass), 78 (reflection), 81 (Hive), 82 (empty machine), 83 (CRT). Their superseded pictures are removed, not relabelled as finished.

TOKYO STORY IN COLOUR — 16:9 full-bleed (1920×1080), no letterbox. Ozu-inspired restraint, NOT black and white: static low-set LEVEL camera, verticals straight, frontal architecture, normal 50mm lens; 35mm only for the aftermath extreme wide. Low camera height never means an upward heroic angle. No tracking, push-in, handheld, Dutch tilt, glamour or action coverage. Modest 35mm Kodak Vision3 500T grain and halation; muted olive, tobacco amber, ivory practicals and wine red. VERA VOSS: preserve sheets/vera.jpg and vera-face.jpg identity, age 29, pale blue eyes, shoulder-length ash-blonde hair with soft fringe. Tonight's wardrobe is her mother's wine-red silk 1990 dress: broad straps, modest draped cowl neck, bias-cut calf-length skirt, no slit; wine-red closed-toe court shoes, low 5cm heels. No coat or handbag on the street. MAKEUP STATES: scene 72 is DRY, carefully groomed and pretty, intact eyeliner/mascara and muted rose-red lipstick, no tear tracks; rain does NOT damage makeup until she steps outside in scene 73. Through the run hair becomes plastered, silk darkens and mascara washes into thin natural trails; retain her face, never horror makeup or a different actress. SHOE LOCK: both shoes until the skid (board shot 74, asset s73/72-the-lost-heel.jpg); thereafter RIGHT foot bare, LEFT red shoe retained. This side is the visual continuity choice, not specified by the screenplay. JACK (48): the private investigator, NOT Daniel Voss and never called Jack Voss. RECAST 25 September 2026 as a white American — follow the regenerated sheets/jack.jpg and jack-face.jpg: tall lean build, long angular face, hollow cheeks, deep-set tired grey-green eyes, dark brown hair swept back and greying at the temples, salt-and-pepper stubble, good but badly kept charcoal knee-length overcoat over open-neck off-white shirt, black trousers and shoes. No tie, hat, gun or cigarette. Coat soaked, hands dark and unwashed after the Hive, non-graphic. He takes the blow, never retaliates, and stops touching her when pushed away. HOTEL LOCK: s72/69-the-wait.jpg — walnut slatted bar, brass rail, oxblood stools, olive wall, piano at left, rain window, amber table lamp; folded pale-blue umbrella remains against the empty neighbouring stool after Vera leaves. STREET LOCK: s73/70-not-elegantly-badly.jpg — ivory vending machine with muted red side panel and right payment panel, dull-green shutter, riveted railway, shallow gutter and drain grate. CONFRONTATION LOCK: s74/74-twenty-metres-apart.jpg — two machines left, awning right, Vera screen-left of Jack until she approaches; cold machine-light and patient rain, no sky fill. Cover the distant stop, approach, chest blow, folding, rejection and final separated kneeling tableau in that order. Reflection is ambiguous, a pale-blue umbrella shape in water only, no resolved ghost or face. Scene 75 has NO PEOPLE, including reflections: same shoe, same puddle; same empty hotel and abandoned umbrella; intact closed Hive, empty vending machine, CRT static. No invented plot text, subtitles or watermarks. All are AI-generated draft studies, not approved coverage.

The call image is a chest-up reframe of its new generation, excluding an invented second counter; the face crop and review contact sheet are derivatives, not extra generations. Exact clock hands and the initial twenty-metre blocking remain production-review checks. The approach keyframe is closer than the initial stop. Scene 76 images remain unchanged.

Scene 72 adds two board positions. Existing shot IDs and asset filenames are stable; their older numeric prefixes are NOT their new displayed board positions. Scene 74 now plays approach, blow/collapse, aftermath wide, reflection, with a return to the wide for the train and late score. The screenplay itself is unchanged.

brainstorm.title: The key
brainstorm.content: A small key on a worn numbered tag — a coin-locker key, pressed into Mara's palm by a dying man with the words don't let them have it. Never explained in the opening, and the reason she is running.

brainstorm.title: Two positions
brainstorm.content: First position done. Moving to second. Second position done. The men work to a list and the film never shows who writes it; the journalist in the bar was already on it, and he had a notebook.

brainstorm.title: The city that lights them
brainstorm.content: Sodium orange against sick fluorescent green: vending machines, shop signs, train windows, a CRT's blue flicker. The sky never does the work, and the rain turns everything black and reflective.

brainstorm.title: Mara, running
brainstorm.content: Twenty-four, American, soaked flat, a cheap enamel red-bird clip holding her hair back, no umbrella, arms folded, halting Japanese. She declines a call, chooses not to run when every instinct says to, and takes the key anyway.

brainstorm.title: Vera's two cups
brainstorm.content: Three days later: one cup of cold tea, one empty and clean, set out as though someone is expected. The answerphone message is an apology, and the umbrella in the stand has never been wet.

brainstorm.title: A clock a minute fast
brainstorm.content: The station is a decade out of step: faded posters, a fax machine beside a flat monitor, and a clock that runs a minute fast. Ishida gives Vera his card at any hour and then closes a drawer on her sister's purse.

script:
Title: Nobody's Witness
Credit: Written by
Author: [Your Name]
Draft date: September 2026

===

>THE LOOK<

Tokyo as a memory that is still happening.

The city in this film belongs to no single year. Pay phones beside smartphones. Boxy CRT televisions glowing in shop windows. Showa-era vending machines humming on empty corners beneath new glass towers. None of it is ever commented on. It is simply how the world is.

LIGHT. The city lights the characters, not the sky: vending machines, shop signs, train windows, fluorescent tubes. Sodium orange against a sick fluorescent green. Soft halation around every light, blacks slightly crushed. It should look like film, and feel like something remembered.

RAIN. Never glamorous. No lightning, no storms. Cold, steady, patient rain that turns the streets black and reflective.

CAMERA. Wide and patient. Close-ups are rare, so they count. We watch people inside the city, not apart from it.

SOUND. Real Tokyo sounds, placed slightly wrong: a crossing melody for an empty street, a television laughing in an empty room. Music arrives late, and sparingly.

OTHER LIVES. There is always a sign of other people -- a lit window, a radio through a wall, laundry overhead. Every private moment happens among thousands of others.

!NOTHING IS EXPLAINED.

LANGUAGE. The Voss sisters speak English to each other. Dialogue marked (in Japanese) is spoken in Japanese and subtitled in English.

REFERENCE POINTS. Ozu's TOKYO STORY for restraint. KOWLOON GENERIC ROMANCE and the 1997 illustrated Kowloon Walled City panoramas for density, texture and memory.

Rain. Not a storm. Just cold, steady, patient rain.

A narrow street of shuttered shops. A vending machine hums on the corner. High up, one lit window, a radio playing behind it.

MARA VOSS (24) stands in the dark doorway of a closed barber's, soaked, no umbrella. Her phone lights up: VERA. She watches it ring.

MARA
(to the phone)
Not tonight.

She declines it.

An OLD MAN (70s) comes slowly up the street in a good coat gone thin at the cuffs. He sees her in the doorway and stops. Something in his face gives way.

OLD MAN
(in Japanese; to himself)
Twenty years.

Behind him, a MASKED MAN steps out of the dark and makes a small, correct bow.

MASKED MAN
(in Japanese; quietly; subtitled: "Excuse me.")
Shitsurei shimasu.

Two shots, flat and small in the rain. The old man folds onto the street.

The masked man touches his ear.

MASKED MAN
(in Japanese)
First position done. Moving to second.

He walks back the way he came, to a dark car idling at the far end of the street. He doesn't hurry. He never looks at the doorway.

Mara runs to the old man. Her bag slides off her shoulder and spills across the wet street. She doesn't notice.

MARA
(whispering)
Mr. Sakai?

MARA
It's okay -- I'll get someone --
(in halting Japanese)
Ambulance. I'll call. Ambulance.

His hand comes out of his coat with something small and brass in it. He presses it into her palm and closes her fingers over it.

OLD MAN
(in Japanese)
Don't let them have it.

MARA
(in halting Japanese)
Have what? I don't --

In her hand: a small brass key on a stamped number tag.

The dark car pulls away and takes the long way round the block. At the other end of the street, the amber glow of a bar. Mara runs for it.

Behind her, on the street: her purse, open in the rain.

(in Japanese; quietly; subtitled: "Excuse me.")

(in Japanese)

(in Japanese)
Second position done.

EXT. VERA'S APARTMENT BUILDING - DUSK

SUPER: "THREE DAYS LATER"

An old four-story apartment block squeezed between newer buildings. Laundry left out on a balcony, getting rained on. A train slides past on the elevated line behind it, windows lit, and the whole building trembles faintly.

One window on the third floor is lit.

INT. VERA'S APARTMENT - CONTINUOUS

Small and tidy. Grey light through rain-streaked glass. A smartphone on the table; an old boxy television in the corner. Nothing here quite belongs to one decade.

By the door, in the umbrella stand: a pale blue umbrella. Bone dry.

On a shelf, one framed photograph, its colors gone warm and faded. A Tokyo street, twenty years ago. An American man in a rumpled suit, smiling, holding the hands of two small girls: VERA (9), serious, and MARA (4), mid-laugh. Behind them, the sign of a noodle shop.

VERA VOSS (29) sits at the low table. Two cups. Hers holds cold tea. The other is empty and clean, set out as though someone is expected.

Through the thin wall, a neighbour's radio plays an old ballad, muffled: a woman's voice, a slow saxophone, a song from another decade. Vera doesn't seem to hear it.

Her phone lies face up in front of her. She calls. Waits.

MARA (V.O.)
(recorded; bright)
It's Mara. You know what to do.

BEEP.

Vera opens her mouth. For a moment, nothing.

VERA
It's me again.
(beat)
I'm not angry anymore. I wasn't really angry then, either. Whatever that man wants, it doesn't matter. I just --
(stops herself)
You left your umbrella. You'll get soaked.
(beat)
Just call me. You don't have to say anything. Just call, so I know.

She hangs up.

The old television murmurs to itself.

NEWS REPORTER (ON TV)
(in Japanese)
...police in Kanda are investigating a double shooting in a small bar in the early hours of Sunday. Two men were killed. Officers say it appears to be a dispute between criminal groups. No arrests have been made...

WEATHER ANNOUNCER (ON TV)
(in Japanese)
...rain continuing through the rest of the week...

She looks at the umbrella by the door. At the clean, empty cup. At the photograph.

She stands. Puts on her coat. Hesitates at the door.

Then she takes the blue umbrella. Mara's umbrella.

The door closes behind her. Through the wall, the song on the neighbour's radio ends. A DJ murmurs something. Rain.

CUT TO:

INT. POLICE STATION, FRONT COUNTER - NIGHT

Fluorescent tubes, one of them flickering. A long counter. Faded posters about pickpockets and traffic safety. An old fax machine beside a new flat monitor. A wall clock that runs a minute fast.

Vera stands at the counter, the closed blue umbrella dripping onto the linoleum.

A YOUNG OFFICER takes her details with polite boredom. Vera's Japanese is fluent, but careful and slightly formal -- learned as a child, relearned as an adult.

YOUNG OFFICER
(in Japanese)
Your sister's age?

VERA
(in Japanese)
Twenty-four.

YOUNG OFFICER
(in Japanese)
Adults sometimes go away for a few days. Especially foreigners. It's usually --

VERA
(in Japanese)
She doesn't. Not without telling me.

He types the name. ON THE MONITOR: MARA VOSS.

He stops typing.

He looks at the screen a moment too long. Then he picks up the desk phone and turns away from her.

YOUNG OFFICER
(in Japanese; quietly, into phone)
Yes. That name. Yes -- the sister is here now.

He hangs up. His manner has changed. Politer.

YOUNG OFFICER (CONT'D)
(in Japanese)
Someone will be right with you.

Vera looks at him. He doesn't meet her eyes.

INT. POLICE STATION, INTERVIEW ROOM - MOMENTS LATER

Small. A table, two chairs, a box of tissues nobody has touched in years. Rain on a frosted window.

DETECTIVE ISHIDA (50s) sets a paper cup of tea in front of Vera. Gentle. Unhurried. Tired, in a way that looks like decency.

ISHIDA
You must be cold.

His English is excellent.

VERA
(in Japanese)
I speak Japanese.

ISHIDA
Of course. But this is a difficult thing. It is easier in your own language.

A small beat. She lets it go. For now.

VERA
The officer looked at the screen and made a phone call. Then you came. What's on the screen?

ISHIDA
Nothing is wrong. We just like to take care with these things.
(sits)
Voss. You grew up here?

VERA
Until I was nine. What's on the screen?

He smiles, as if she has passed a small test.

ISHIDA
When did you last see your sister?

VERA
Three days ago. At my apartment. We had dinner.

ISHIDA
And how did she seem?

Vera hesitates.

VERA
(too quickly)
Normal.

Ishida waits, kindly, as if he knows there is more. She doesn't give it.

ISHIDA
Did she ever mention Kanda? Friends there? Work?

Vera's eyes go to the frosted window before she answers.

VERA
Kanda? No. Why --

She stops. Something arrives in her face.

VERA (CONT'D)
The shootings. In Kanda. It was on the news.

Ishida says nothing. That is its own answer.

VERA (CONT'D)
Is she hurt?

ISHIDA
We have no reason to believe she is hurt.

VERA
That's not the same as saying she isn't.

ISHIDA
Miss Voss --

VERA
Is she dead?

ISHIDA
We have no reason to believe she is dead.

She hears it: the careful, official shape of the sentence. Her hand tightens around the paper cup.

VERA
Stop saying that. Stop saying what you have no reason to believe and tell me what you know.

ISHIDA
What I know is that two men were killed in Kanda, and that it is a matter between criminal groups. And that your sister is a young woman who has not called her sister for three days.
(beat)
Those may be two separate things.

VERA
May be.

ISHIDA
May be.

The cup crumples in her fist. Hot tea runs over her fingers and onto the table. She doesn't seem to feel it.

For the first time in years, someone takes a tissue from the box. Ishida does, and offers it to her. She doesn't take it. He sets it down beside her hand.

When she speaks again, it's in Japanese. Low. Precise. Every word placed.

VERA (CONT'D)
(in Japanese)
She is my sister. I have been calling her for three days. If you know where she is, tell me.

Ishida looks at her a long moment. And when he answers, it is in Japanese too, for the first time. Formal. Quiet. A door closing.

ISHIDA
(in Japanese)
I do not know where she is. That is the truth.
(beat)
And if she saw something she should not have, then the safest place for her is wherever she is now. And the safest thing you can do is nothing.

Silence. Rain on the frosted window.

He switches back to English, gentle again, as if the last minute didn't happen.

ISHIDA (CONT'D)
Go home, Miss Voss. Keep your phone on. If she calls, call me first. Any hour.

He slides his card across the wet table. She looks at it. Then takes it. Stands. Picks up the blue umbrella.

At the door:

VERA
You would have told me if she was dead. Wouldn't you?

ISHIDA
Of course.

She looks at him. She can't tell. She goes. The door closes behind her.

Ishida sits alone a moment. He wipes the spilled tea from the table with the tissue, slowly, carefully, until there is no trace of it.

INT. POLICE STATION, DETECTIVES' ROOM - CONTINUOUS

Rows of cluttered desks under humming fluorescent light. Most are empty at this hour. A radio plays low somewhere.

Ishida sits at his desk and opens the bottom drawer. The two drawers above it stay closed.

Inside the drawer, sealed together in one clear evidence bag: Mara's purse and the torn strap, coiled beside it. Still damp.

.BACK TO SCENE

He looks at it a long moment. Closes the drawer.

On the wall, the clock runs a minute fast.

INT. SMALL BAR, KANDA - DAY

The same bar in flat grey daylight. It looks smaller without the night. Chairs up on the counter. The CRT television is dark.

Where the journalist fell, there is a new rubber floor mat, too clean for this room.

OKADA (60s), the bar's owner, mops around it without looking at it. He has the stillness of a man who hasn't slept.

The door opens. Vera, the blue umbrella in her hand.

OKADA
(in Japanese; not looking up)
We're closed.

Vera holds up her phone: a photo of Mara, laughing at a party, a paper crown on her head.

VERA
(in Japanese)
My sister. Four nights ago. Was she here?

Okada looks at the photo for exactly one second.

OKADA
(in Japanese)
No.

VERA
(in Japanese)
You didn't look.

OKADA
(in Japanese)
I looked. No.

His eyes go, just once, to the far end of the counter. Then back to the mop.

Vera sees it. She doesn't push. She bows, small and polite, and leaves.

She has left the blue umbrella leaning against a stool.

Okada looks at the umbrella for a long moment.

EXT. KANDA STREET - CONTINUOUS

Rain. Vera walks away down the narrow street, no umbrella, head down.

OKADA (O.S.)
(in Japanese)
Miss.

She turns. Okada stands in the bar doorway holding the blue umbrella, out of breath, as if deciding something cost him more than the walk.

He hands it to her. Then he holds out his other hand. In it: the small red enamel bird clip.

Vera stops breathing.

VERA
It was mine. She took it when we were kids. She never gave it back.

She has said it in English, without realizing. Okada doesn't understand the words. He understands her face.

OKADA
(in Japanese)
Behind the counter. After.

VERA
(in Japanese)
Did you give this to the police?

OKADA
(in Japanese)
They didn't ask.

He takes a business card from his apron and presses it into her hand. Old, soft at the corners, handwritten on the back.

OKADA (CONT'D)
(in Japanese)
Not the police. Him.

VERA
(in Japanese)
Who is he?

OKADA
(in Japanese)
He found my daughter once. When no one else would look.

He goes back inside before she can thank him.

Vera looks at the card. Printed in English and in katakana: JACK. INVESTIGATIONS. An address. No surname.

INT. JACK'S OFFICE - NIGHT

Second floor of an old building pressed against the elevated railway. One room. Frosted glass door, JACK hand-lettered on it in English and in katakana.

A desk. A black rotary phone. Filing cabinets. A small CRT television on the cabinet, muted, playing an old black-and-white samurai film. A sofa that has clearly been slept on.

A TRAIN passes outside. The blinds shiver. A spoon rattles in an empty cup. Then silence again.

JACK (48) sits at the desk eating a convenience-store rice ball, watching the silent swordsmen. Handsome once, in a way he stopped maintaining. A good coat, badly kept. He flicks an old steel lighter open and shut, open and shut. There are no cigarettes anywhere.

A knock on the frosted glass. Vera comes in, wet, the blue umbrella dripping.

VERA
(in Japanese)
Are you the one they call Jack?

JACK
(in Japanese)
Who calls me that?

VERA
(in Japanese)
Mr. Okada. The bar in Kanda.

Jack puts the rice ball down.

JACK
(in Japanese)
Sit down.

She sits. He doesn't switch to English. He lets her speak in the language she chose. She notices.

VERA
(in Japanese)
My sister has been missing for four days. The police say to go home and wait.

JACK
(in Japanese)
I don't do missing persons. People who go missing usually want to.

She places the red bird clip on his desk.

VERA
(in Japanese)
She was in that bar. The night two men were shot there.

Jack looks at the clip for a long moment. The lighter stops.

JACK
(in Japanese)
What did the police tell you?

VERA
(in Japanese)
To go home.

JACK
(in Japanese)
It's good advice.

VERA
(in Japanese)
Is it yours, too?

He doesn't answer. Another train passes. The blinds shiver.

JACK
(in Japanese)
Do you have photographs of her?

She takes an envelope from her bag. As she pulls out the photos, something slides out with them and falls face up on the desk:

The old framed photograph from her shelf, taken out of its frame. Twenty years ago. The American man in the rumpled suit. The two small girls. The noodle shop sign behind them.

Jack looks at it.

He does not move. On the TV behind him, a sword is drawn in total silence.

VERA
That's us. Before we left.

She has slipped into English. So does he, quietly.

JACK
Your father.

VERA
He died. That year. Here.

Jack picks the photograph up by its edges, carefully, the way you'd handle evidence. Or something fragile. He looks a moment too long at the noodle shop sign. Then he sets it down, face up, and squares it to the edge of the desk.

JACK
I'm sorry.

VERA
It was a long time ago.

JACK
Yes.

A beat.

JACK (CONT'D)
Ten thousand yen a day. Plus expenses. I'll need a key to her apartment, her phone number, her friends, where she worked, where she drank.

VERA
So you'll look.

JACK
I'll look.

She gathers the photographs. Leaves the red bird clip where it is. He doesn't give it back, and she doesn't ask.

At the door, she stops.

VERA
Mr. Okada said you found his daughter.

JACK
I found her.

VERA
Was she alive?

Jack looks at her. The honest answer is in the pause.

JACK
Her Japanese. Your sister's. Is it good?

VERA
Some. Badly.

JACK
Then she stands out. That helps.

Vera nods. Goes. Through the frosted glass, her shape goes down the stairs and is gone.

Jack sits very still.

INT. JACK'S OFFICE - LATER

Past midnight. Only the desk lamp and the grey flicker of the television, now showing static.

Jack crouches at the grey steel cupboard under the window, pulls its door open and takes out a cardboard box he has kept behind the files. Dust on the lid. He hasn't opened it in years.

Inside: a police notebook. An old ID card with a younger face. A folded newspaper clipping.

.INSERT - THE CLIPPING

An English-language newspaper, yellowed. A small headline: AMERICAN INSURANCE INVESTIGATOR FOUND DEAD - POLICE RULE SUICIDE. A photograph: the same man from Vera's picture. The caption: DANIEL VOSS, 41.

.BACK TO SCENE

Beneath the clipping, one more photograph. Two men at a tiny noodle counter, laughing, steam in the air: DANIEL VOSS, and a much younger JACK, still in a cheap police-issue suit.

Behind them, the same noodle shop sign.

Jack looks at it for a long time.

Then he dials the rotary phone. It takes a long time to dial.

ISHIDA (V.O.)
(in Japanese; filtered)
It's late, Jack.

JACK
(in Japanese)
The Voss girl came to see me.

ISHIDA (V.O.)
(in Japanese)
I know.

Silence on the line. Rain on the window.

JACK
(in Japanese)
Her sister was in that bar.

ISHIDA (V.O.)
(in Japanese)
The sister is a missing persons case. The bar is a gang matter. Two separate things.

JACK
(in Japanese)
And the old man in the street?

ISHIDA (V.O.)
(in Japanese)
Sakai.
(beat)
Yes. That Sakai. I know what you're thinking. Old debts, old enemies. It's a gang matter.

JACK
(in Japanese)
Twenty years, Ishida.

A long pause.

ISHIDA (V.O.)
(in Japanese; gently)
Go to sleep, Jack. You found enough twenty years ago. You're too old to be haunted.

The line goes dead.

Jack holds the receiver a moment longer. He sets it down. Flicks the lighter open. Shut.

A train passes. The photograph of the two laughing men trembles on the desk.

EXT. BACKSTREET, KANDA - NIGHT

The street from the cold open. The rain hasn't stopped in four days.

Jack walks it slowly, a cheap clear plastic umbrella over his head. Not searching. Looking.

The vending machine at the corner. He feeds it a coin. A can of hot coffee drops.

VENDING MACHINE
(recorded; in Japanese)
Thank you very much.

He holds the can without drinking it and looks at the spot where Sakai died. Nothing there now. Rain on asphalt.

He turns and looks at the barbershop doorway. Steps into it. Stands exactly where Mara stood.

From here, he can see the whole street. And, at the far end, the small lit sign of Okada's bar.

He looks at the barbershop pole beside him. Crouches.

Caught on a rough metal edge at knee height: a short twist of torn leather strap.

He doesn't touch it. He looks from the strap, to the spot where Sakai fell, to the bar sign. Reconstructing it.

A shutter RATTLES up above him. A BARBER (80s), in pajamas, looks down from the upstairs window.

BARBER
(in Japanese)
Police again?

JACK
(in Japanese)
Not for a long time.

The barber considers him.

BARBER
(in Japanese)
I told them. I was asleep. I heard the shot. Then a car.

JACK
(in Japanese)
One car?

BARBER
(in Japanese)
One car. Twice.
(beat)
It left. Then it came back.

Jack looks down the empty street.

JACK
(quietly, in Japanese)
Why come back?

Jack doesn't answer. He looks down the street at the drains, the doorways, the gutter: everywhere a small thing could fall.

The barber shrugs and pulls the shutter down.

He looks again at the doorway. At the bar sign. At the torn strap.

She was here. She saw it. She ran there. She saw that too.

And whatever they came back for, she has it.

He looks down the empty street at the bar sign. And one more question he can't answer yet: what was an American girl doing in a Kanda backstreet at one in the morning?

Jack drops the unopened coffee into the recycling bin. The can CLANKS. The crossing melody starts up somewhere, for no one.

INT. MARA'S APARTMENT - DAY

A tiny studio in an old building. Grey daylight. Clothes on every surface. Sketches taped to the walls: pencil, charcoal, cheap watercolour. Trains. Rooftops. Laundry lines. Faces on the subway.

The room smells of someone who meant to come back.

Vera stands just inside the door. She hasn't taken her coat off. Jack moves through the room slowly, touching nothing yet. Looking.

JACK
When were you last here?

VERA
A week ago. She made me coffee. It was terrible.

Jack opens the fridge. Milk. A half-eaten cake in a box. He closes it.

JACK
She wasn't planning to disappear.

VERA
No.

He crouches by the futon. A suitcase underneath, packed and zipped. He looks at it, then at Vera.

VERA (CONT'D)
That was for America. She'd booked a flight. Next month.

JACK
You didn't want her to go.

VERA
I didn't want her to run away again.
(beat)
That's what I said. The night she left. That she always runs.

She looks at the wall of drawings, not at him.

VERA (CONT'D)
It was about Dad. It's always about Dad. She wanted to dig it all up. Who he was here. Why he --
(beat)
I told her to leave him dead.
(beat)
She said I was the one who ran. All the way back here, chasing a ghost, and I won't even look at it.
(beat)
I told her to go, then. Go home. Those were the last things I said to her.

Jack says nothing. He knows better than to comfort it away.

On the desk: a thick sketchbook, its cover soft with use. Jack opens it.

Page after page of the same place. A tiny noodle counter under a railway. Six stools. A curtain. A hand-painted sign. Drawn over and over, from different angles, in different years of her hand -- a child's crayon version taped inside the cover, the newest in careful ink.

JACK
She drew this a lot.

Vera glances over.

VERA
Since she was little. It's from a story I used to tell her. About the noodle shop Dad took us to. She was too young to remember it, so I told her.
(small smile)
She made it up from what I said. It's not real.

Jack turns a page. The sign, in careful ink. Every stroke of the kanji correct.

He has seen this sign. Twice this week. Once in a photograph on Vera's shelf. Once in a box in his own cupboard.

JACK
Can I borrow this?

VERA
Why?

Jack doesn't answer. He looks at the drawing a moment too long.

Vera takes the hair clip out of her coat pocket and sets it on the sketchbook.

VERA
Take this too. It's mine. She stole it.

He takes both.

She hesitates, then nods. He closes the sketchbook and puts it under his arm, and says nothing else about it.

EXT. THE HIVE - DAY

Rain. A wide street of new glass towers and chain stores.

Between two towers, a long white construction hoarding: KUROSE DEVELOPMENT, and a painted plaza full of smiling people who don't exist. Behind it, low and dark and patched, the Hive.

A dense, self-built block of stacked homes and workshops rising eleven storeys, balconies bolted onto balconies, air conditioners and pipes and laundry and hand-painted signs, all of it crushed together under the curve of the elevated railway. The city has grown up around it and forgotten it is there.

At the back, the tower steps down to a low rear wing pressed hard against the concrete railway viaduct, its roof level with the tracks. Old neon signs hang dead on its face. Even in daylight the Hive sits in its own haze of steam and kitchen smoke, as if it had its own weather.

Jack stands on the pavement with the sketchbook under his coat. He looks up at the Hive for a long moment, as if at someone he used to know.

Then he goes in.

INT. THE HIVE, PASSAGES - CONTINUOUS

Narrow corridors, barely shoulder-wide, lit by bare bulbs. Water drips from somewhere above and runs along the floor in a thin shining line. Pipes overhead. Wires everywhere. What daylight gets in comes in thin cold shafts from gaps far overhead, thick with drifting steam.

Doors stand open onto other lives. A MAN at a bench mending radios, a dozen of them murmuring different stations at once. A FAMILY eating dinner at four in the afternoon, the TV loud. An OLD WOMAN asleep in front of a sumo match. A dentist's chair behind a curtain, a hand-lettered price list taped to the wall.

Jack walks through it all. Nobody stops him. Everybody sees him.

A TRAIN passes overhead. The whole building trembles. Dust sifts down through the bulb light. Nobody looks up.

He turns a corner and stops.

The noodle counter. Six stools. The curtain. The hand-painted sign, faded almost to nothing but unmistakable.

It is exactly the drawing.

INT. KANEKO'S NOODLE COUNTER - CONTINUOUS

Steam. A single fluorescent tube. Two customers slurping in silence at the far end.

Behind the counter, KANEKO (70s), tiny and sharp-eyed, works a pot with long chopsticks. She looks up as Jack sits on the fourth stool, beside the third.

She looks at him for a long time. Longer than a stranger would.

KANEKO
(in Japanese)
You got old.

JACK
(in Japanese)
So did you.

KANEKO
(in Japanese)
I was already old. You were a boy in a cheap suit, the only foreign face on the force. Japanese papers, American face. You came here with the American.
(beat)
You always sat there. He sat there.
(beat)
Everything is going. We are just slower.

She looks at the empty third stool beside him.

Jack looks at the third stool, empty beside him, and then at the counter under his hands.

JACK
(in Japanese)
I'm looking for his daughter. The younger one.

Kaneko's chopsticks don't pause.

KANEKO
(in Japanese)
The little one? She was four years old. She ate rice with her fingers.

JACK
(in Japanese)
She's twenty-four now. And someone wants to kill her.

The two customers at the end of the counter have stopped slurping.

Kaneko sets a bowl of noodles in front of Jack.

KANEKO
(in Japanese)
Eat. Then go.
(beat)
There is no one here but us.

Jack eats. Slowly. He finishes everything.

He puts down more money than the bowl costs, far more, and a business card on top of it.

JACK
(in Japanese)
He always paid too much, too.

He goes. Kaneko looks at the card for a long moment.

Behind the curtain, in the dark of the storeroom, something moves.

INT. JACK'S OFFICE - NIGHT

Rain. The old television plays static. Jack sits in the dark, the sketchbook open on the desk.

He turns to the last page. Tucked inside the back cover: a letter, folded small, creased as though it had been crumpled into a ball and smoothed flat again.

He unfolds it under the lamp. Cheap lined paper. Careful, laborious English handwriting.

.INSERT - THE LETTER

"Miss Voss. Your father did not kill himself. I can prove it. I have kept his papers for twenty years. I am old and I am ill and I do not want to carry them any more. Please telephone." A phone number. The signature: T. SAKAI.

.BACK TO SCENE

The envelope folded inside it is addressed to VERA VOSS.

Jack reads the letter twice. Then he looks at the name on the envelope for a long time.

The black rotary phone RINGS.

He answers. Listens.

KANEKO (V.O.)
(in Japanese; filtered)
Come back. Alone. After the last train.

The line clicks dead.

INT. KANEKO'S NOODLE COUNTER - NIGHT

Past midnight. The shutter half down. The fluorescent tube is off; only a single bulb burns.

Kaneko lifts the curtain to the storeroom and stands aside.

INT. THE HIVE, NOODLE SHOP STOREROOM - CONTINUOUS

Flour sacks. The futon. The bare bulb.

MARA sits on the futon with her knees up and her phone to her ear, listening.

VERA (V.O.)
(filtered)
You left your umbrella. You'll get soaked.
(beat)
Just call me. You don't have to say anything. Just call, so I know.

The message ends. She plays it again.

Jack is in the doorway. She scrambles back against the wall.

JACK
My name is Jack. Your sister hired me.

MARA
Prove it.

Jack sets her sketchbook on a flour sack between them, with the hair clip on top.

Mara stares at it.

JACK
She says it was hers. She says you stole it when you were kids and never gave it back.

Something in Mara's face gives way.

MARA
It was never hers. Dad gave it to me. She just says that.

She pulls the sketchbook into her lap.

She almost laughs, and then she is crying, silently, pressing the back of her wrist against her mouth.

Jack waits. He doesn't go to her. He sits down on a flour sack, slowly, making himself smaller.

MARA
Is she okay? Is she -- does she know you're --

He doesn't answer. So she asks again.

MARA
Is she okay?

JACK
She's been calling you. She hasn't slept.

MARA
I know. I listen to them.

JACK
Why were you in Kanda, Mara?

She looks at him. Decides.

MARA
He wrote to Vera. Mr. Sakai. She threw it in the bin without even answering. I took it out.
(beat)
I called him. He said he had Dad's papers. He said to come to the bar at one o'clock. There'd be a man from a newspaper there too, so it couldn't be buried again.
(beat)
I sent them both a photo so they'd know me. He wrote back one line. "You have his face."

JACK
Vera doesn't know you went.

MARA
We had a fight about it. I called her a coward.
(small, bitter laugh)
And I'm the one hiding in a storeroom.
(beat)
Don't tell her I'm here.

JACK
She's your sister.

MARA
They have my purse. My passport. They know my name. They know where I live, where she lives, all of it. If she knows where I am, she'll come here. She won't be able to help it. And they'll follow her.
(beat)
They'll use her to get to me. And then they'll kill her too.

JACK
You don't know that.

MARA
I watched them shoot two men like they were switching off lights.

Silence. The bulb hums.

MARA (CONT'D)
Promise me.

Jack looks at her for a long moment. Twenty years of silence sit behind his eyes.

JACK
I promise.

INT. JACK'S OFFICE - DAY

Grey light. Rain on the window. Jack hasn't slept. He is in yesterday's shirt.

Footsteps on the stairs. The frosted glass. Vera's shape.

She comes in carrying two coffees in paper cups. She puts one on his desk.

VERA
You look terrible.

JACK
Thank you.

She sits. She doesn't take her coat off. She waits.

VERA
Did you find anything?

The sketchbook is on the desk between them. Jack's hand rests on its cover.

A train passes. The blinds shiver.

JACK
Not yet.

She nods. Believes him. That's the worst part.

VERA
Okay.
(beat)
Okay. Tomorrow, then.

She stands. At the door she hesitates, as though she wants to say something else. She doesn't. She goes.

Jack sits very still. He picks up the coffee she brought him and holds it without drinking, the way he held the can at the vending machine.

INT. ALL-NIGHT NOODLE COUNTER, UNDER THE TRACKS - NIGHT

A different place: a narrow standing-and-stools counter wedged into a brick railway arch. A ticket machine by the door. Yellowed menus on the wall. A radio behind the counter plays baseball, low.

11:40 p.m. by the clock over the door.

Vera and Jack sit side by side at the counter. Empty bowls. Two coffees in thick white cups. They have been here a long time.

Every few minutes, a train rumbles overhead, and the cups tremble in their saucers.

VERA
He used to bring us somewhere like this. Dad. After work. Mara would fall asleep on the counter and he'd carry her home.

JACK
And you?

VERA
I stayed awake. I wanted to hear everything he said to the man who made the noodles. I didn't understand any of it. I just liked that he was different here. Lighter.
(beat)
I think he was happy here. Before.

Jack looks down at his cup.

VERA (CONT'D)
They said he killed himself. My mother never talked about it. Not once. We went home and it was as if Tokyo never happened.

JACK
Do you believe it?

She thinks about it for a long time.

VERA
I believe he was sad. I don't know if I believe the rest.
(beat)
A man wrote to me last week. He said Dad didn't do it. He said the police knew.

Jack keeps his eyes on his bowl.

JACK
(carefully)
What did you do?

VERA
I threw it in the bin.
(beat)
Because if it's true, then someone did it. And nobody looked. Twenty years, and nobody even looked.

Jack is very still. The letter is in the inside pocket of his coat. He doesn't move to touch it.

A train. The cups tremble.

VERA (CONT'D)
You're very easy to talk to. It's annoying.

JACK
I get paid to listen.

VERA
You're not getting paid right now.

He has no answer to that.

She rests her head on her folded arms on the counter. Just for a moment. Her eyes close.

VERA (CONT'D)
(barely awake)
You're the first person I've trusted since she disappeared. Did you know that?

Jack looks at her. His mouth opens. The truth is right there.

JACK
Vera --

But she is asleep.

He sits and watches her breathe. A train passes. Her coffee cup, near her elbow, trembles toward the edge of the counter.

He reaches over and moves it back from the edge. Carefully. Quietly. So it won't wake her.

He doesn't wake her. He sits there until the counterman begins stacking chairs.

EXT. YAKITORI STALL, UNDER THE TRACKS - NIGHT

Smoke. Red paper lanterns. Salarymen at plastic tables under a railway bridge, talking too loud.

Ishida sits alone at a corner table with a beer and a plate of skewers. Jack sits down opposite him.

ISHIDA
(in Japanese)
You never call me unless you want something.

JACK
(in Japanese)
Sakai.

Ishida sighs. Turns a skewer over with his chopsticks.

ISHIDA
(in Japanese)
You already know what he was. In the bubble years he cleared land. Old tenants who wouldn't sell. First he'd bring flowers. Then he'd bring men. Then something would happen. A fire, sometimes.

JACK
(in Japanese)
The Shiohama fire.

ISHIDA
(in Japanese)
Among others.
(beat)
The journalist in the bar was from the Toto Shimbun. He'd been asking about the redevelopment money. Who owns what. Whose friends vote on what. The usual. Sakai called him a week ago. We think Sakai wanted to confess something before he died. He had cancer. Months left.

JACK
(in Japanese)
Confess what?

ISHIDA
(in Japanese)
Who knows. An old man's conscience. It's very common.

Jack watches him.

JACK
(in Japanese)
Why are you telling me all this?

Ishida puts down his chopsticks.

ISHIDA
(in Japanese)
Because you'll find out anyway. And because I would rather you heard it from me than from someone who wants to hurt you.
(beat)
Twenty years ago I told you to sign that report. You were young. You did what your senior told you. That was on me, not on you.

JACK
(in Japanese)
I still signed it.

ISHIDA
(in Japanese)
And I've carried it too. Every day.
(beat)
Whatever Sakai hid, Jack, if you find it, bring it to me. Not to the department. To me. I'll know what to do with it this time.

JACK
(in Japanese)
Sakai had a wife.

ISHIDA
(in Japanese)
Separated. A fishing town on the Boso coast. The police have spoken to her. She gave us nothing.

He takes a napkin, writes an address on it in careful longhand, and slides it across the table. Nothing in his face at all.

A long pause. A train roars overhead. The lanterns sway.

Jack nods slowly.

It is exactly what he needed to hear. That is what makes it dangerous.

INT. THE HIVE, NOODLE SHOP STOREROOM - NIGHT

The bulb. The flour sacks. Mara sits cross-legged on the futon. Jack sits against the opposite wall.

The curtain moves. Kaneko brings in a bowl of rice, steam rising into the bulb light.

KANEKO
(in Japanese)
Eat.

MARA
(in halting Japanese)
Thank you. Has anyone... come? Asking?

KANEKO
(in Japanese)
Nobody comes here who isn't lost.

She puts the bowl in Mara's hands. The curtain falls shut behind her.

The rice goes cold in Mara's lap. They talk quietly, as if the building is listening. It is.

MARA
Mr. Sakai said "twenty years." Before they shot him. Like he'd been expecting them for twenty years.

JACK
He probably had.

MARA
He knew me. He saw me in the doorway and stopped. And at the end he pressed the key into my hand. "Don't let them have it."

Jack looks down at his hands.

Beside the futon, held down by a flour scoop: a stack of loose pages covered in pencil. He turns the top one toward the bulb.

A drawing from floor level. The underside of a counter. A crate of bottles. Two pairs of shoes. A stool going over. An outflung hand. In the corner, small: 1:07. Beside the shoes, in her careful block capitals: EXCUSE ME.

JACK
You drew this.

MARA
It's the only thing I know how to do with it. If I don't put it on paper it just keeps happening.
(beat)
That's what he said when he came into the bar. "Excuse me." Like a customer. He said it in the lane too, before --

She doesn't finish.

Jack sets the page down exactly where it was.

MARA (CONT'D)
And then in the bar, the man said, "Where is he?" He was waiting for the old man. They were supposed to meet.

JACK
Sakai was bringing him something.

Mara opens her fist. The coin-locker key on its worn tag.

MARA
This.

Jack takes it. Turns it over under the bulb. The number on the worn tag, still legible: 114.

JACK
It's not a station locker. They clear those every three days.

MARA
Then what is it?

JACK
Somewhere he paid for. For a long time.

He hands it back. She looks surprised.

JACK (CONT'D)
Keep it. Until I know what it opens. It's safer with you than with me.

MARA
Why?

JACK
Because nobody knows where you are.

Mara closes her hand around the key. She looks at him properly for the first time.

MARA
Is she eating?

JACK
What?

MARA
Vera. She forgets to eat when she's upset. She just drinks coffee. Is she eating?

Jack thinks of the counter at 11:40 p.m. The empty bowls.

JACK
Last night she had noodles.

MARA
Good.
(beat)
Make her eat breakfast. She never eats breakfast.

INT. TINY BREAKFAST COUNTER, NEAR THE STATION - MORNING

A coffee counter no wider than a corridor. Six seats, a glass siphon bubbling over a flame, toast cut as thick as a paperback. A CRT on the shelf shows a morning cooking show, sound low. The window is fogged from the inside.

Vera sits with her coat still on and her phone face up beside her, already looking at the door as though the day has started without her.

Jack sets a plate down in front of her: thick toast, a boiled egg, a small dish of pickled cabbage that nobody asked for.

VERA
What's this?

JACK
Breakfast.

VERA
I don't eat breakfast.

JACK
You drink coffee until the afternoon and then you forget to eat.

VERA
Has someone been reporting on me?

He says nothing. She looks at the plate. She looks at him. She picks up the toast, mostly to end the conversation.

VERA (CONT'D)
You sound like my sister.

Jack's hand stops on his cup.

Vera doesn't see it. She is looking at the cooking show.

VERA (CONT'D)
She used to stand over me with a plate. Twenty-four years old, bossing me around my own kitchen.
(beat)
She'd have liked you. She likes anyone who's stubborn.

JACK
She sounds like she was right.

VERA
Was.
(beat)
Is. I keep saying was.

JACK
(quietly)
Is.

She bites the toast. Chews. Her face changes, the way a person's face does when she finds out she was hungry.

She eats the egg. She eats the cabbage. On the television a chef lifts a lid and steam fills the frame.

Jack watches her eat, the way he watched her sleep. It is the easiest hour he has spent in twenty years, and he knows exactly what it is costing.

She wipes her fingers on a paper napkin.

VERA
Thank you.

JACK
For what?

VERA
For making me.

She reaches for her purse. He is already at the till, paying. Too much. The woman behind the counter doesn't mention it.

INT. YAMANOTE LINE TRAIN - DAY

A green-striped commuter train circling the city. Rain on the windows. Afternoon light, grey and soft. The carriage is half empty: schoolkids, an old man asleep, a woman with shopping.

Vera and Jack sit side by side. Nowhere to go. Just riding the loop.

VERA
Dad used to do this when he couldn't think. Ride the whole loop. An hour. He said Tokyo was a clock and the Yamanote was the second hand.

JACK
Did it help?

VERA
I don't know. He did it a lot at the end.

The train sways. Her shoulder settles against his.

She takes his hand without asking and turns it over. The old steel lighter is in his palm; he has been flicking it without knowing.

She takes it. Opens it. Closes it. Opens it.

VERA (CONT'D)
You don't smoke.

JACK
I quit.

VERA
When?

JACK
Twenty years ago.

VERA
And you still carry the lighter.

JACK
Habit.

VERA
That's not a habit. That's a promise you don't trust yourself to keep.

He looks at her. She has no idea how true that is.

She tries to give it back. He closes her fingers around it.

JACK
Keep it.

VERA
Why?

JACK
Because I quit.

She looks at the lighter in her hand. Then she puts it in her coat pocket. And her head comes to rest on his shoulder, as if it has always belonged there.

Out of the window, Tokyo circles past. Rooftops. Laundry. Rain.

EXT. PEDESTRIAN CROSSING - DAY

A small intersection.

Rain.

The crossing signal turns green and the old melody begins to CHIME.

Vera and Jack cross in the rain, laughing at something, sharing his cheap plastic umbrella that's too small for two. Her shoulder gets wet. His gets wet. Neither of them cares.

WIDE: two small figures crossing an empty road while the city's old song plays for them.

INT. SMALL BAR, KANDA - DAY

The bar in daylight again. The rubber mat is still there, still too clean. Okada is polishing a glass that is already polished.

Vera comes in without the umbrella this time. Okada sees her and doesn't say we're closed.

VERA
(in Japanese)
Mr. Okada. You said he found your daughter.

Okada goes on polishing.

OKADA
(in Japanese)
She was fifteen. She went to Osaka with a boy. Everyone said she was gone. He found her in three weeks.
(beat)
He didn't bring her home. She didn't want to come. He told me where she was, and he told me not to go. Write, he said. Wait.

VERA
(in Japanese)
Was he right?

OKADA
(in Japanese)
She has two children now.
(beat)
I hated him for a year.

He sets the glass down.

OKADA (CONT'D)
(in Japanese)
He finds things. And then he carries them by himself. I have never seen him put anything down.

VERA
(in Japanese)
Is that a warning?

OKADA
(in Japanese)
It's a description.

Vera looks along the counter, to the far end, where his eyes went the first time.

VERA
(in Japanese)
Show me where.

Okada lifts the counter flap: the gap between the crates and the ice bin.

She goes through. Crouches behind the far end, between the crates and the shelves, exactly where Mara crouched. She sees what Mara saw: the underside of the counter, the crate of empty bottles, the place where the stool went over, the dark screen of the television on the ceiling.

VERA (CONT'D)
(in English; to herself)
She was here.

OKADA
(in Japanese)
I was in the back. Moving crates.
(beat)
I heard all of it. I stood there with a crate in my arms and I did not move. That is why I gave you the clip.
(beat)
He said "excuse me" when he came in. Like a customer.

Vera stays where she is on the floor.

VERA
(in Japanese)
She would have stayed very still. She has never been still in her life.

OKADA
(in Japanese)
People learn.

Vera looks up at the dead television. Somewhere in the dark glass, her own face.

For the first time she lets herself think it clearly: her sister saw two men die, and has not called.

Okada takes a card from his apron and sets it on the counter. TOTO SHIMBUN. The journalist's name in katakana: KONDO.

OKADA (CONT'D)
(in Japanese)
He left it the week before. He said he was meeting someone. He said it would be a good week.
(beat)
I couldn't call them. I couldn't say what I heard.

Vera takes the card.

EXT. FISHING TOWN, BOSO COAST - DAY

Grey sea. Grey sky. Rain on the slipway. Boats pulled up on a concrete slipway. A single road of low houses, their paint scoured by salt wind.

Jack's old car, parked on the sea wall. He gets out, pulls up his collar against the wind, and walks.

INT. MRS. SAKAI'S HOUSE - DAY

A small room. A kotatsu table. A television with the sound off. A Buddhist altar in the corner: a new photograph of Sakai, younger, smiling in a way that doesn't suit him.

MRS. SAKAI (70s), small and hard, pours Jack tea she doesn't want to pour.

MRS. SAKAI
(in Japanese)
We haven't lived together in fifteen years. The police already came.

JACK
(in Japanese)
I'm not the police.

MRS. SAKAI
(in Japanese)
Then what are you?

Jack thinks about it.

JACK
(in Japanese)
Someone who owes a man a debt. A long time ago. The same kind of debt your husband owed.

She studies him. Then she looks at the photograph on the altar.

MRS. SAKAI
(in Japanese)
He started going to temple last year. Him. Temple. He sat there for hours. I thought he'd gone soft in the head.
(beat)
Last month he wrote a letter. In English. Him. He made me check the spelling. To an American girl.
(beat)
When the doctor told him, he said he was glad. He said now he could stop being afraid of the wrong thing.

JACK
(in Japanese)
Did he ever pay rent on something? Somewhere that wasn't his home?

She looks at him sharply.

MRS. SAKAI
(in Japanese)
Every January. Cash, in an envelope. Twenty years. Even after he left, the receipts kept coming here.
(beat)
He left these here. Maybe on purpose.

She takes a rubber-banded bundle of receipts from the altar drawer. Carbon copies, handwritten, yellowed. The top one: KATO RENTAL LOCKERS, UENO.

Jack unfolds it. A rubber stamp, faded. Handwritten: No. 114. Paid in full.

He looks up. She is watching him with an expression he can't read. Grief, maybe. Or relief.

MRS. SAKAI (CONT'D)
(in Japanese)
Whatever it is, it was heavier than me. He carried it longer.


EXT. COUNTRY HIGHWAY - NIGHT

Rain. Black fields. Jack's old car, one headlight dimmer than the other, the only thing moving for miles.

Ahead, a light. A sign on a pole, half its bulbs dead: a roadside inn.

EXT. ROADSIDE INN - NIGHT

Two storeys of weathered wood and a tin roof, set back from the highway behind a gravel lot. A beer vending machine glowing by the entrance. A faded sign. The kind of place that was modern once, in about 1975.

A pickup truck, older than the building's paint, is parked crooked behind it.

Jack pulls into the lot. The only car.

INT. ROADSIDE INN, LOBBY - CONTINUOUS

A small, warm, faded room. A pink public payphone on the wall. A glass case of souvenir keyrings nobody has bought in decades. A CRT television on a shelf showing a night baseball game, the crowd murmuring.

MRS. NODA (70s) comes out from the back, drying her hands. MR. NODA (70s) doesn't look away from the baseball.

MRS. NODA
(in Japanese)
Just one night?

JACK
(in Japanese)
Just one.

She hands him a heavy old key on a wooden tag.

MRS. NODA
(in Japanese)
Upstairs, at the end. The bath is shared, I'm sorry. I'll show you. The light doesn't work properly.

INT. ROADSIDE INN, CORRIDOR AND BATH - CONTINUOUS

She leads him down a narrow wooden corridor. Past the kitchen: pots, a steel counter, a back door with a bolt.

MRS. NODA
(in Japanese)
Kitchen. If you want tea, just take it. The back door sticks. My husband says he'll fix it. He's said so since the Olympics.

JACK
(in Japanese)
Which Olympics?

MRS. NODA
(in Japanese)
Exactly.

She opens a door: a small tiled bathroom, a deep wooden tub, one high window over it, fogged with steam and swollen shut in its frame.

MRS. NODA (CONT'D)
(in Japanese)
If it's too steamy, the window opens. If you hit it hard enough.

Jack notices the window. He notices everything. That is the point of the scene, and nobody in it knows it.

INT. ROADSIDE INN, JACK'S ROOM - NIGHT

Tatami. A low table. A thin futon already laid out. Rain loud on the tin roof.

Jack sits at the table with Sakai's receipts spread out in front of him under the lamp. KATO RENTAL LOCKERS - UENO. No. 114. Twenty years of Januaries.

He takes out his phone. No signal.

INT. ROADSIDE INN, LOBBY - NIGHT

Mr. Noda asleep in front of the baseball. Jack at the pink payphone, feeding it coins.

INTERCUT WITH:

INT. VERA'S APARTMENT - NIGHT

Vera on the floor with her back against the bed, the apartment dark around her. Her phone rings. Unknown number. She answers fast.

VERA
Mara?

JACK (V.O.)
It's me.

A beat. Disappointment, then something else.

VERA
Where are you? You sound like you're calling from 1985.

JACK
The coast. An inn off the highway. The phone is pink.

She almost laughs.

VERA
Did you find anything?

Jack looks at the receipts in his hand.

JACK
Maybe. I'll know tomorrow.

VERA
Come back safe.

JACK
It's just an inn. There's an old couple and a baseball game.

VERA
Come back safe anyway.

He hears her breathing on the line. Neither of them hangs up.

The coins run out. The line goes dead.

Vera looks at the phone. Jack looks at the payphone. Both of them hold on a moment longer than they need to.

INT. ROADSIDE INN, KITCHEN DOORWAY - NIGHT

Jack can't sleep. He wanders back down the corridor.

The kitchen's back door stands open to the rain. Mrs. Noda sits on the step outside under the eave, smoking.

MRS. NODA
(in Japanese)
Don't tell my husband.

JACK
(in Japanese)
I quit.

MRS. NODA
(in Japanese)
Then you'll understand why I don't want him to know.

She offers the pack anyway. He shakes his head. He stands in the doorway and looks out: a muddy yard, a gate onto a farm track, and the old pickup parked crooked across the path.

MRS. NODA (CONT'D)
(in Japanese)
Sorry about the truck. He parks it like he's drunk. He's never drunk. The keys are always in it. Who would steal that?

Jack looks at the truck. He says nothing.

EXT. ROADSIDE INN - NIGHT

Later. 2 a.m. Rain.

The highway. Empty. Then headlights.

One car. Two. Three. Four. Black sedans, one after another, slowing, turning in, gravel crunching.

INT. ROADSIDE INN, JACK'S ROOM - CONTINUOUS

Jack's eyes open in the dark. He has heard the gravel.

He goes to the window. Lifts one corner of the thin curtain.

HIS POV THROUGH THE CURTAIN GAP: four black cars in an arc across the lot, headlights on, rain visible only inside the beams. Eight MEN step out, two from each car. Black clothes. Masks. Compact submachine guns held low and easy.

They don't rush. They split without speaking. Two toward the entrance. Two around the back. Two toward the side. Two stay by the cars.

Jack lets the curtain fall.

He moves fast and quietly: sweeps the receipts into his jacket, pulls on his shoes, takes nothing else.

Downstairs, the baseball crowd CHEERS on the TV.

INT. ROADSIDE INN, LOBBY - CONTINUOUS

The front door opens. Two masked men step in, weapons up.

The first is the MASKED LEADER (40s), a man in a plain dark suit, nothing about him to remember. His face stays behind the mask. The man who touched his earpiece in the Kanda rain.

Mr. Noda wakes in his chair. Stares.

MR. NODA
(in Japanese)
We're closed --

A burst of suppressed fire into the ceiling. Plaster rains down. Mr. Noda throws himself behind the counter.

The souvenir case shatters. The CRT keeps playing baseball.

INT. ROADSIDE INN, UPSTAIRS CORRIDOR - CONTINUOUS

Jack at the top of the stairs. He hears boots below. He goes the other way, toward the bath.

Behind him, a masked man reaches the top of the stairs and fires down the corridor. The paper screens along one wall burst apart in a line of holes.

Jack is already through the bathroom door.

INT. ROADSIDE INN, BATHROOM - CONTINUOUS

Dark. Steam still hanging. Jack climbs onto the edge of the deep tub and hits the swollen window frame with the heel of his hand. Once. Twice. It won't move.

Boots in the corridor.

The third time, he hits it with everything he has. The frame cracks open. Rain pours in.

He hauls himself through.

EXT. ROADSIDE INN, KITCHEN ROOF - CONTINUOUS

A low slope of wet tin below the bathroom window. Jack drops onto it, slides, catches the gutter, and swings down --

INT. ROADSIDE INN, KITCHEN - CONTINUOUS

-- through the open back door into the kitchen, where Mrs. Noda is crouched on the floor behind the steel counter, rigid with fear.

He grabs her arm, pulls her low toward the pantry, opens it, puts her inside.

JACK
(in Japanese; whispered)
Stay. Whatever you hear.

MRS. NODA
(in Japanese; whispered)
My husband --

JACK
(in Japanese; whispered)
I'll get him.

He closes the pantry door on her.

He moves up the corridor toward the lobby, keeping low along the wall.

INT. ROADSIDE INN, LOBBY - CONTINUOUS

From the corridor, Jack can see the lobby. One masked man stands in the middle of the room, weapon up, covering the stairs. The other has gone up.

Mr. Noda is behind the counter, out of the gunman's line of sight. He sees Jack. Jack puts a finger to his lips.

Jack reaches out and flips the lobby light switch. DARK.

Only the TV lights the room now: blue, flickering.

The masked man spins and fires toward the corridor. The shots stitch across the wall above Jack's head. One tears through the beer vending machine by the door.

It lights up and CHIMES:

VENDING MACHINE
(recorded; in Japanese)
Thank you very much.

The gunman flinches toward the sound.

In that half-second, Jack is across the dark lobby, behind the counter. He grabs Mr. Noda by the collar and drags him down the corridor.

On the wall, the pink payphone starts to RING.

No one answers it. It rings and rings.

INT. ROADSIDE INN, KITCHEN - CONTINUOUS

Jack pushes Mr. Noda into the pantry beside his wife. The old couple clutch each other in the dark.

Jack looks at them.

JACK
(in Japanese)
I'm sorry.

He shuts the door. He goes out the back.

EXT. ROADSIDE INN, BACK YARD - CONTINUOUS

Rain. Mud. The farm gate. The pickup truck.

A masked man comes round the side of the building. Sees him.

Jack runs. Gunfire kicks up mud behind him. He dives behind the truck. Bullets punch through the bodywork above his head, through the tailgate, through a wheel.

He yanks open the driver's door and pulls himself in, flat along the seat.

INT. PICKUP TRUCK - CONTINUOUS

The keys are in the ignition, exactly where she said.

He turns them. The engine coughs. Dies.

The windscreen cracks as a round goes through it.

JACK
(under his breath)
Come on. Come on.

He turns the key again. The engine catches. Roars.

EXT. ROADSIDE INN, BACK YARD - CONTINUOUS

The truck lurches forward and smashes through the farm gate. Two masked men throw themselves aside. The truck fishtails through the mud onto the farm track, then onto the highway.

The eight men walk out into the lot, one by one, and stand in the headlights of their cars, watching the single red taillight shrink into the rain.

They don't chase him. They don't need to.

The MASKED LEADER touches his earpiece.

MASKED LEADER
(in Japanese)
He's gone. He has what she gave him.

Behind them, inside the lobby, the pink payphone is still ringing.

INT. PICKUP TRUCK - MOVING - DAWN

Grey light. Empty highway. Rain through the shattered windscreen.

Jack drives with one hand. Blood runs from his hairline down the side of his face. His shirt is dark with it at the shoulder.

He looks in the mirror. No one.

He reaches into his jacket. The receipts are still there, soaked and creased.

He breathes. Only now does his hand start to shake.

Then the thought arrives, and his face changes.

Only two people knew where he was going tonight. He counts them silently.

Ishida. He asked Ishida for the widow's address.

And Vera. He called her from a pink payphone and told her it was just an inn.

He drives on. The wipers beat. He doesn't want to think it. He thinks it anyway.

INT. CHAIRMAN'S OFFICE, KUROSE DEVELOPMENT - DAWN

The fortieth floor. Glass on three sides. Tokyo spread out below in the rain like a circuit board. The glass walls grey with dawn. Nobody in the leather chairs.

The model of the redevelopment on its long table: glass towers, sponge trees, a broad white plaza. At the plaza's edge sits one small, dark, patched block, out of place among the towers. The Hive.

A man's hand, clean, with an expensive watch, lifts the Hive out of the model and sets it on a tray beside a cup of tea.

The plaza underneath is already finished. Tiny painted people cross it.

INT. VERA'S APARTMENT - DAWN

A knock at the door. Vera opens it in a sweater, barely awake.

Jack. Soaked. Blood dried down the side of his face.

VERA
Oh my God.

She pulls him in.

INT. VERA'S APARTMENT, BATHROOM - CONTINUOUS

A small tiled bathroom. Jack sits on the closed toilet. Vera kneels in front of him with a bowl of warm water and a cloth, cleaning the cut at his hairline.

He watches her face while she works. Very closely. As though he is trying to read something written there.

VERA
Who did this?

JACK
I don't know.

VERA
You don't know?

JACK
Two that I saw. Masks. They didn't introduce themselves.

She wrings out the cloth. Pink water.

VERA
You told me it was just an inn.

JACK
It was just an inn.

Jack's eyes go to Vera's phone on the edge of the bath, where it has sat all night in case Mara calls. He stops.

She looks up and catches him watching her.

VERA
What?

He doesn't answer. He's still watching. Measuring. She sees something in his look that she doesn't understand, and it frightens her more than the blood.

VERA (CONT'D)
Jack. What?

He looks at her hands: careful, steady, stained pink. At her face: exhausted, afraid for him.

Whatever he was looking for, it isn't there. It was never there.

JACK
Nothing.
(beat)
I'm sorry. Nothing.

She puts a plaster on the cut, very gently. Her hand stays on his face a moment after.

He covers her hand with his.

And then, without either of them deciding, she kisses him. Or he kisses her. It doesn't matter which.

It is quiet, and brief, and it changes everything.

When it ends, she rests her forehead against his.

VERA
Don't go anywhere else without telling me.

JACK
I won't.

When she turns to wring out the cloth, he reaches over and turns her phone face-down.

It is another promise. He is collecting them.

INT. TOTO SHIMBUN NEWSROOM - DAY

An old newspaper office. Stacks of paper. Desks jammed together. Televisions on the walls showing three different channels. Nobody under fifty looks up from a screen.

Vera stands at the door of a glass-walled office at the back, KONDO's card in her hand. HARADA (50s), the editor, grey-haired, sleeves rolled, is finishing a call. She sees the card and ends it without hurry.

On her desk, a framed photograph of the journalist from the bar, laughing at an office party.

HARADA
(in Japanese)
You're not a reporter.

VERA
(in Japanese)
My sister was in that bar.

Harada looks at her for a long time. Then at the photograph. She points at the chair.

HARADA
(in Japanese)
We have had a letter from lawyers already. Kondo was six months on the redevelopment money. Who owns what. Whose friends sit on which committee. He never touched a gang in his life.

VERA
(in Japanese)
The police say it's a gang matter.

HARADA
(in Japanese)
The police say what they are told.

VERA
(in Japanese)
Did he say who he was meeting?

HARADA
(in Japanese)
One o'clock, Kanda, an old man who wanted to talk. He told two people. Me. And a detective.

VERA
(in Japanese)
Which detective?

HARADA
(in Japanese)
He didn't say. He said the detective had promised to keep a car nearby.
(beat)
There was no car.

Vera sits very still.

VERA
(in Japanese)
Will you print it?

HARADA
(in Japanese)
Print what? A dead man's diary?
(beat)
Bring me something with a name on it.

Vera writes her number on the back of Kondo's card and leaves it on the desk, beside the photograph.

EXT. OLD TOBACCO KIOSK - DAY

A tiny kiosk wedged into the corner of a shopping arcade. An OLD TOBACCONIST (80s) behind a window full of cigarette cartons and lottery tickets.

Vera holds up the old photograph. The American man, two small girls, the noodle shop sign.

VERA
(in Japanese)
My father worked near here, a long time ago. Do you know this place?

The tobacconist puts on his glasses. Looks. Smiles with all his remaining teeth.

OLD TOBACCONIST
(in Japanese)
Kaneko's. Of course. In the Hive.
(beat)
Not for long, though. They're knocking it all down.

Vera stares at him.

VERA
(in Japanese)
It's still there?

OLD TOBACCONIST
(in Japanese)
Everything is still there. Until it isn't.

INT. THE HIVE, PASSAGES - DAY

Vera walks through the narrow corridors with the photograph in her hand, looking at everything as though she's trying to remember it. Bare bulbs. Dripping water. The radio repairman's dozen murmuring stations. Daylight falls in thin cold shafts through the steam.

At a turning she stops, then takes the left without looking, the way you take a stair you've climbed a thousand times. A hand-painted sign for a DENTIST, one flight up. A RADIO REPAIRMAN at his bench under a bare bulb glances up at her and back down. Through a half-open door, an OLD WOMAN watches sumo on a television the size of a bread box.

Vera puts her hand flat on the wall, low, where a child's hand would reach.

A train passes overhead. The building trembles.

She stops. Turns a corner.

The noodle counter. The sign.

She stands there for a long moment, holding the photograph up beside the real thing. They match.

INT. KANEKO'S NOODLE COUNTER - CONTINUOUS

Lunchtime. Steam. Three customers.

Vera sits at the counter.

Kaneko turns from the pot, sees her, and freezes. Just for a second. Then she goes on working.

VERA
(in Japanese)
I'm sorry, I don't know what to order. I was here when I was a child. With my father. He always sat here.

Kaneko looks at her for a long moment.

KANEKO
(in Japanese)
He always paid too much.

Vera's breath catches.

VERA
(in Japanese)
You remember him?

KANEKO
(in Japanese)
Your father used to sit on the third stool.

Vera looks at it. She moves along to it and sits.

KANEKO
(in Japanese)
And you. You ate everything on his plate.

She sets a bowl of noodles in front of Vera. Vera looks at it. Her eyes fill.

INT. THE HIVE, NOODLE SHOP STOREROOM - CONTINUOUS

On the other side of the curtain, three feet away.

Mara stands pressed against the wall with both hands over her mouth. She has heard her sister's voice. She is shaking.

Through the thin gap at the edge of the curtain she can see the back of Vera's head. The third stool.

Mara takes one step toward the curtain. Her hand lifts to it.

She stops.

She thinks of the purse in the rain. Of the two men falling. Of her sister being followed through these corridors.

Her hand drops.

INT. KANEKO'S NOODLE COUNTER - CONTINUOUS

Vera eats. All of it. She laughs once, at nothing, wiping her eyes.

VERA
(in Japanese)
My sister would love this place. She's never seen it. She only knows it from my stories.
(beat)
When I find her, I'll bring her here.

Kaneko's chopsticks stop moving in the pot. She doesn't look up.

KANEKO
(in Japanese)
Yes. Bring her.

Vera puts money on the counter. Too much. Kaneko notices and says nothing.

Vera goes, lighter than she has been for the whole film.

Behind the curtain, Mara slides down the wall to the floor.

EXT. THE HIVE - CONTINUOUS

Rain. By the Hive's narrow entrance, under a tin awning, a green public payphone. JACK stands at it with the receiver to his ear. It's ringing.

INTERCUT WITH:

INT. MRS. SAKAI'S HOUSE - SAME

The kotatsu. The altar. The television on with the sound off. A teacup on its side on the tatami. The phone rings in the empty room.

EXT. THE HIVE

Vera comes out of the Hive's narrow entrance, glowing.

VERA
Jack! It's still here. The noodle shop from the photo. It's real. The same woman -- she remembered Dad. She remembered me.

Jack keeps the receiver to his ear. It rings.

VERA
And I went to the newspaper. Harada, the editor. She says Kondo told two people about the one o'clock. Her. And a detective, who promised to keep a car nearby.

JACK
Later.

VERA
Jack. A detective.

JACK
Later. Please.

It rings. Nobody answers. He hangs up.

VERA
When we find Mara, I'm bringing her here. She'll finally see it.

JACK
Yes.

INT. THE HIVE, NOODLE SHOP STOREROOM - NIGHT

The bulb. Mara sits on the futon with her knees pulled up. Her face is swollen from crying. On the wall beside her, taped up with rice-paper tape: a new drawing, still smudged. The noodle counter from behind the curtain. The back of a head on the third stool.

Jack crouches in front of her.

MARA
She was right there. She was right there and I --

JACK
You did the right thing.

MARA
Did I?
(beat)
She said she'd bring me here. When she finds me. She was so happy.

She wipes her face with the heel of her hand.

JACK
If she found this place, other people can.

MARA
I know.

MARA (CONT'D)
Find what it opens. And then this ends. I don't want to hide any more. I want my sister.

She takes the key from around her neck, on a shoelace, and puts it in his hand. Its worn tag reads 114.

JACK
Tomorrow night I'm moving you out of here. Somewhere safe, outside Tokyo. A police car and a house. Someone I trust.

MARA
And then?

JACK
And then I tell her everything.
